First release. The JuiceFS S3 gateway as a container you can install from a template, with the file system created on first boot.

## ✨ Added

- The JuiceFS S3 gateway on port 9000, running the official binary. Upstream publishes no image meant to be installed as a container: their Docker volume plugin is not a container and cannot come from an Unraid template, and `juicedata/mount` expects the full command line by hand. This image reads its settings from the environment instead, so each one is a field in the template.
- The file system is created the first time the container starts. A bare install with no settings at all comes up serving S3, which is otherwise a `juicefs format` in a console before anything can be used.
- An existing file system is left alone on every later start. The check runs before the format step, because formatting a second time would orphan every object already in the store. The build has a test for exactly this: it starts the container, restarts it on the same volumes, and fails if the volume UUID changed.
- One field decides where the metadata lives. `META_URL` defaults to a SQLite file in the config folder, which needs no second container and is captured by a backup of that folder. A Redis or Postgres URL in the same field moves the metadata to a database that several machines can share.
- The object store is a plain directory by default. `STORAGE` and `BUCKET` take every backend JuiceFS supports, so the chunks can go to another S3 server, to B2 or to MinIO instead of the local disk.
- Leaving the secret key empty generates one and writes it to `/config/.s3_root_password`. The container log says so and points at the file, so an install that skipped the field is still usable.
- The binary is taken from the upstream release and checked against the published SHA256 during the build, rather than copied out of a third-party image. A re-tagged release fails the build instead of shipping.
- s6-overlay supervises the gateway, and a ready banner in the log marks the end of the first start.
- Images for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64.

## ⚡ Improved

- The README states that the data folder is not browsable, and the template overview repeats it before install. JuiceFS stores files as chunks under its own layout, so anyone expecting to read the folder with a file browser wants VersityGW instead. Saying it once in a footnote would be too late.
- Backup guidance sits in both places as well: the metadata database and the object store belong together, from the same point in time. The chunks cannot be read without the database, so a backup of only the data folder is not a backup.
